task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of December 9, 2024. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Okonkwo family's domestic well in Prospect Valley went dry in June 2024 after 31 years of reliable service; the water table in their zone of the Prairie Basin Aquifer has dropped 9 meters in eight years.

Nkechi Okonkwo, 58, said the well failure happened without warning: the pump ran dry on a Tuesday morning while she was washing dishes; she did not realize the well was failing because there was no gradual decline.
Okonkwo said: "I had to ask a neighbor to bring water in a tank. We have a house and a yard and we're living like it's 1890. You don't expect that in this county."
The county has 340 registered domestic wells drawing from the Prairie Basin; water district records show 28 of them reported yield problems or failure in 2024, compared to four in 2019.
Water district engineer Mark Dahl said the failures are concentrated in wells drawing from the upper 40 meters of the aquifer, where the water table has dropped fastest.
Dahl said: "These aren't agricultural wells. These are people's drinking water. When they fail, there is no backup. They were never designed to have a backup."
Drilling a new deeper well costs between $18,000 and $35,000; the Okonkwos received a $12,000 county emergency assistance grant but said the gap is beyond their immediate means.
The county has a $1.4 million annual fund for domestic well assistance; it has received 47 applications in 2024 and has capacity to fund approximately 20 at average grant levels.
Okonkwo said she applied in August and as of December has not received a decision; the county said applications are reviewed in order of submission but some require additional documentation.
Three of Okonkwo's neighbors — all with shallow wells — have drilled deeper and recovered water; one neighbor said her total drilling cost was $29,000 and took seven weeks.
Dahl said the deeper aquifer zones are also declining, but more slowly; without agricultural extraction reductions in the region, deeper zones will eventually follow the shallow zones.

The dominant aquifer users in Prospect Valley are irrigated corn farms; a 2023 state-commissioned study found that reducing irrigated corn acreage by 20% would meaningfully slow the aquifer's decline rate.
No extraction reduction program has been implemented; the state legislature has twice declined to expand water district authority to regulate domestic well zones.
Okonkwo said she attends county water board meetings and has been told the problem is complex: "They say 'complex.' I say I have no water. Those are not the same conversation."
Dahl said the district's authority is limited to distributing surface water and assisting with well repairs; it cannot regulate groundwater extraction without additional legislative authorization.

A state water policy attorney said that domestic well users in most western states are the least protected class of water right holders, with no priority over agricultural or municipal users in times of shortage.
Okonkwo said she is thinking about moving: "We own this house. We've been here thirty years. But a house without water is not a home."

Dahl said the 28 failures in 2024 represent a turning point: prior to this year, well failures were isolated enough to treat case by case; at current rates, the problem will require a systemic response.
A hydrologist contracted by the county said the Prairie Basin's decline rate is accelerating and that absent policy change, domestic well failures will reach 60 to 80 per year by 2027.
Okonkwo said she has not changed her view that the county government is trying: "They're trying. They just don't have what it takes to actually fix it."
